text:
Gevo has announced plans to double its ethanol production capacity in North Dakota by expanding operations at the former Red Trail Energy ethanol plant site, according to North Dakota Monitor.

The company will set up a second production unit with a capacity of up to 75 million gallons of low-carbon ethanol annually. This is in addition to its earlier plan to increase the capacity of the existing plant from 67 million gallons to 75 million gallons per year.

Company officials said North Dakota continues to be a preferred location for expansion due to its strong agriculture and energy base. The presence of carbon capture and storage infrastructure at the site has also supported the decision to invest further.

The facility was the first in the United States to capture carbon dioxide during ethanol production and store it underground nearby. This system helps the company access tax benefits and supports its plans to produce cleaner fuels in the future.

Gevo, which acquired the plant in 2024, said the expansion will also help lay the groundwork for sustainable aviation fuel production. The company has shifted its focus to North Dakota after putting similar plans in South Dakota on hold.

The expanded plant is expected to require a significant amount of corn, with estimates suggesting annual usage of nearly 52 million bushels. This represents a portion of the state’s total corn output, which stood at around 711 million bushels last year.

The development comes as the Environmental Protection Agency has allowed the sale of gasoline with up to 15% ethanol during the summer and set higher blending targets for biofuels.

The project is subject to approval from state authorities, and the company has not yet shared details on the investment size or timeline.

text:
Executive Summary

Biomethane is central to the European Union's strategy to decarbonise its gas system while leveraging existing infrastructure. Despite reaching approximately 4.9 bcm (=52 TWh) of production in 2023 and ambitious targets of 35 bcm by 2030 under the REPowerEU Plan, the development of a truly pan-European biomethane market faces significant structural barriers. Industry commitment remains strong, with the European Biogas Association (EBA) identifying €28 billion in allocated investments projected to deliver 7.3 bcm per year of biomethane capacity by 2030.

However, national export restrictions and physical bio-LNG exports-requirements for physical delivery that discriminate against mass-balance accounting, and fragmented certification systems prevent the emergence of a liquid cross-border market. The legality of such restrictions under EU law, particularly principles of non-discrimination and internal market freedoms, remains a critical unresolved question. Meanwhile, FuelEU Maritime is creating significant new demand for bio-LNG in maritime transport, yet national restrictions on bio-LNG bunkering risk fragmenting this emerging market.

This article reflects the policy and market landscape as of January 2026. Given the rapidly evolving nature of EU biomethane regulation, readers should verify current legal provisions and national implementation timelines.

1. Introduction: The Promise and Reality of EU Biomethane

By the end of 2023, EU biomethane production had reached approximately 4.9 bcm (~52 TWh), marking an 18% increase compared to 2022. With installed capacity of around 7 bcm per year and more than 1,600 biomethane plants operating across 25 Member States by end-2024, the sector has demonstrated substantial growth momentum.

The REPowerEU Plan has set an ambitious, albeit non-binding, EU-level target of 35 bcm (=350 TWh) of biomethane production by 2030-a nearly sevenfold increase from 2022 levels. According to the EBA Biomethane Investment Outlook (June 2025), €28 billion has been allocated to invest in biomethane production, projected to deliver 7.3 bcm per year of capacity to Europe by 2030. Of this total, €26 billion is designated for developments within Europe: €7.5 billion in 2025-2026, with another €17.7 billion for 2027-2030.

However, biomethane production remains highly concentrated geographically. In 2022, the most mature EU markets were Germany (13 TWh), Denmark and France (6 to 7TWh.. Although annual biomethane production in Spain in 2022 stood at only 0.5 TWh, Spain is set to become one of the leading biomethane producers in the EU with the potential to satisfy the 2030 national 20TWh annual biogas production target entirely from biomethane production.

Developing a genuine pan-EU biomethane market requires enabling biomethane produced in one Member State to be traded, certified, and used for compliance purposes in another, whilst avoiding double counting and ensuring coherent interaction between production and demand-side incentives. Today, several structural concerns stand in the way of this vision such that less than 5% of biomethane is consumed outside its country of origin.

2. Core Challenges to Market Integration

2.1 Regulatory Fragmentation and Divergent National Approaches

The 35 bcm target for 2030 is non-binding at EU level, leaving implementation to individual Member States. This has resulted in divergent national strategies, creating significant uncertainty for investors.

Absence of an EU-Wide Blending Standard

As of 2026, there is no single EU-wide mandatory green gas blending standard. While the EU has established a comprehensive regulatory framework through the Hydrogen and Decarbonised Gas Market Package-consisting of Regulation (EU) 2024/1789 and Directive (EU) 2024/1788-it relies on voluntary targets, certification systems, and national-level mandates rather than a unified blending percentage for the entire bloc. EU countries have until 24 February 2027 to fully transpose these directive rules into their national laws.

In the absence of an EU-wide standard, individual Member States are developing their own blending mandates: the Netherlands is implementing a blending obligation starting 1 January 2027, Austria aims to substitute nearly 10% of gas volume with renewable gases by 2030, and France's green gas obligation is expected to become effective in 2026.

This patchwork of national approaches creates fragmentation, as national production subsidies and support schemes typically mandate that subsidised biomethane be consumed domestically to meet national renewable energy and climate targets. Consequently, the renewable value and greenhouse gas reduction benefits of biomethane generally cannot be exported to other Member States, fundamentally undermining the development of cross-border trade.

Sector-Specific Mandates

Certain sectors have specific, binding requirements: Aviation (ReFuelEU Aviation, Regulation (EU) 2023/2405) established a 2% Sustainable Aviation Fuel mandate beginning in 2025, rising to 6% by 2030; Maritime (FuelEU Maritime, Regulation (EU) 2023/1805) sets GHG intensity reduction targets for ships from 2025. Further, EU ETS2 (operational by 2027 or 2028) will extend to road transport with biomethane qualifying for zero-rated treatment if it meets RED II/ III sustainability criteria.

2.1.1 FuelEU Maritime and Bio-LNG Bunkering: A Critical Demand Driver

Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 on the use of renewable and low-carbon fuels in maritime transport (FuelEU Maritime) entered into force in 2025 and represents one of the most significant demand-side drivers for biomethane. FuelEU Maritime establishes progressively stricter greenhouse gas intensity limits for energy used on board certain ships calling at EU ports: 2% reduction in 2025, increasing to 6% by 2030, 14.5% by 2035, 31% by 2040, and 80% by 2050.

The regulation applies to ships above 5,000 gross tonnage calling at EU ports, covering approximately 50% of energy used during voyages to/from EU ports and 100% of energy used at berth.

Bio-LNG Advantages

Bio-LNG offers "drop-in" compatibility with existing LNG-fuelled vessels without engine modifications; achieves 65-90% GHG emission reductions compared to fossil marine fuels; can leverage existing LNG bunkering infrastructure with modest modifications; and serves as a near-term compliance pathway while lower-carbon e-fuels achieve necessary scale.

FuelEU Maritime is expected to create substantial new demand for biomethane in bio-LNG form. Manure-based biomethane can achieve negative emission values under FuelEU Maritime which can create a compliance surplus that shipowners can bank for future years or monetise through pooling arrangements with other operators.

Denmark's position as the largest biomethane exporter is partly driven by maritime demand, with Danish producers benefiting from higher prices in the bunkering market. Demand will be concentrated at major EU ports-Rotterdam, Antwerp, Zeebrugge, Hamburg, Barcelona, Algeciras, Marseille, Piraeus.

National Restrictions as Barriers

France's bio-LNG export restrictions: Subsidised biomethane cannot be liquefied at French LNG terminals for use outside the country; French bio-LNG must be exported via mass-balancing to other terminals in the EU. This means French ports (Marseille, Dunkirk, Montoir-de-Bretagne) cannot become major bio-LNG bunkering hubs for subsidised biomethane, despite France being the largest biomethane producer in Europe by capacity.

Physical delivery requirements: The Netherlands' draft Fuel Transition Obligation which transposes RED III requires bio-LNG to be "unsubsidised, certified, and physically delivered" to qualify for domestic compliance. This discriminates against mass-balance bio-LNG produced at foreign EU terminals (e.g., Zeebrugge) using biomethane from Dutch or other EU sources.

In contrast, Belgium's Zeebrugge terminal and the Netherlands' Gate terminal in Rotterdam have successfully implemented mass-balance bio-liquefaction for export and maritime bunkering. Spain, with €4.8 billion in planned biomethane investments and over 50 plants in development, is positioning itself as a future renewable gas export and maritime hub.

2.2 Certification, Traceability, and Cross-Border Guarantees of Origin

A unified biomethane market requires interoperable systems for Guarantees of Origin (GOs) and Proofs of Sustainability (PoS). The distinction between these two instruments, and the chain-of-custody systems underlying them, has become increasingly important.

Chain-of-Custody Systems

Mass Balance System: Requires that sustainable and non-sustainable materials can be mixed (e.g., in the gas grid), but the sum of all quantities withdrawn and described as having sustainability characteristics must match the quantities added. Article 27 of RED II (maintained in RED III) explicitly recognises mass balance as an acceptable verification method.

Book-and-Claim System: Allows the environmental attributes of renewable energy (represented by certificates) to be traded separately from the physical commodity, with no requirement for physical flow.

Regulatory Distinction: PoS certificates must follow mass balance rules for regulatory compliance (RED III targets, ETS obligations, FuelEU Maritime). GO certificates can be traded on a book-and-claim basis for consumer disclosure, but if issued alongside a PoS for the same gas batch, they must remain bundled.

PoS vs GO Certificates

PoS certificates prove that green gas meets RED III sustainability and GHG saving requirements. They are linked to physical gas flow through mass balance, contain granular data including feedstock, production pathway, and specific GHG emission factor, are issued by economic operators under Commission-recognised schemes (ISCC, REDcert, CertifHy), and must remain bundled with GOs if both are issued for the same gas batch.

GHG Emission Data Mandatory - includes detailed E-values (specific GHG emission factors) Optional or limited detail Issuer

Voluntary certification schemes recognised by the European Commission (e.g., ISCC, REDcert, CertifHy)

Must remain bundled with PoS if both are issued for the same gas batch

Not sufficient alone for regulatory compliance

Overlapping Certification Systems

Two partially overlapping certification frameworks coexist: ERGaR (European Renewable Gas Registry) for grid-injected biomethane, operational in the UK, Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, France, and others; and AIB (Association of Issuing Bodies) historically developed for renewable electricity, now extending to gases. Spain's Enagás uses AIB for integrated biomethane and hydrogen tracking.

This dual-system architecture creates critical problems: GOs issued in ERGaR registries may not be automatically recognised or transferable to AIB registries, forcing producers and buyers to choose between systems. ERGaR-to-ERGaR transfers take 5-10 working days; ERGaR-to-AIB transfers often require manual processes, extending timelines to 25 days or more and increasing transaction costs.

Divergent national rules compound these problems: Germany and Austria restrict who can cancel GOs within each jurisdiction; France restricts biomethane GO exports to "ex-domain cancellation" rather than direct registry-to-registry transfer, creating legal and commercial uncertainty; Spain uses AIB, creating interoperability challenges with ERGaR-dominant markets. These issues reduce liquidity, increase transaction costs, and affect project bankability. To avoid such issues, certain Member States, such as the Netherlands, are members of both frameworks

2.3 Union Database Implementation and Upstream Traceability

The Union Database for Biofuels (UDB) is designed as a central compliance mechanism for tracking sustainability and preventing fraud. As of 2026, the UDB is becoming the mandatory traceability tool for all renewable gases in the EU. By 2026, transactions must be registered in the UDB to ensure a fully traceable chain of custody from feedstock origin to final consumption.

The delegated regulation extending UDB traceability to upstream raw materials was adopted by the European Commission in late 2025. In parallel, the Commission is finalising a revision of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/996 on sustainability certification, expected to be finalised by the end of 2026, to introduce powers to retroactively cancel PoS certificates if fraud is detected.

Critically, the UDB will not automatically remove national export restrictions or physical delivery requirements. The UDB is designed as a traceability and compliance tool, not to dictate how Member States design subsidy schemes or export conditions. UDB creates technical capacity for seamless cross-border traceability, but Member States retain discretion over support schemes and domestic use requirements.

2.4 National Subsidies and Trade Restrictions

Most biomethane today is produced under national schemes that prohibit the export of "renewable value" to other Member States. Subsidised biomethane is effectively locked into national markets to fulfil domestic renewable and climate targets. Many of these restrictions are designed to prevent ‘double compensation’ – the practice of receiving a production subsidy in one country and then selling

the ‘green value’ as a compliance ticket in another country. The primary driver for these restrictions is the EU State Aid Guidelines, which prohibit "overcompensation." The UDB is the EU’s primary digital tool to automate the detection of double subsidies for biomethane by registering every transaction throughout the biomethane value chain and once a unit of biomethane has been registered

against a national target of one Member State, the UDB automatically retires that volume thereby preventing it from being used to fulfil a mandate in another Member State.

France: Export Restrictions

Certificate-Side Restrictions: French biomethane can only be exported via "ex-domain cancellation"-the cancellation of renewable gas guarantees of origin (RGGOs) in the French registry for use in a different country's system. This mechanism "carries risk to buyers, as ownership is not necessarily transferred." There is no standard EU-wide registry link ensuring secure transfer of ownership rights.

Physical Export Restrictions: Subsidised biomethane cannot be liquefied at French LNG terminals for use outside the country. France's restrictions directly undermine FuelEU Maritime's effectiveness. French ports-strategically positioned for Mediterranean and Atlantic shipping routes-cannot become major bio-LNG bunkering hubs using subsidised French biomethane, diverting bunkering activity to Belgium, the Netherlands, and potentially Spain.

Policy Context: France's biogas/biomethane production is supported by a state-guaranteed tariff reaching up to €120/MWh. The Biogas Production Certificate (CPB) blending mandate began in January 2026 and can be satisfied through domestic production only and CPBs cannot be imported or exported. France has delayed transposition of RED III and the new GHG-based IRICC ticket system to 2027.

Comparative Position

Netherlands: Second-largest exporter. The Gate terminal has produced bio-LNG for export using mass balance re. Germany: Largest importer, with exports limited by economics rather than legal bans, although German subsidised biomethane cannot be exported to other registries for ‘double counting’ in foreign transport mandates and biomethane that has received production subsidies in its country of origin is disqualified from generating German THG-Quota tickets. Belgium: Zeebrugge terminal has successfully implemented bio-liquefaction based on mass balance. Spain, Italy, Poland: No documented export prohibitions comparable to France's.

2.5 Physical Delivery Requirements and the Legality Question

RED II and RED III explicitly recognise mass balance as a legitimate chain-of-custody system for renewable fuels. However, some Member States have introduced or are considering domestic compliance systems that require physical delivery of biomethane rather than recognition of mass-balance accounting.

The Netherlands: Although a pioneer in biomethane export and successful user of mass balance for bio-LNG production at the Gate terminal, concerns have emerged regarding its domestic RED III implementation. Dutch market participants have criticised the proposed Fuel Transition Obligation for requiring bio-LNG to be unsubsidised, certified, and physically present at the point of liquefaction or delivery to qualify for ERE tickets, effectively discriminating against mass-balance bio-LNG produced at foreign EU terminals as well as the ‘greening’ of fossil LNG that is physically located at a terminal in the Netherlands linked to GOs in respect of an equivalent quantity of biomethane injected into the interconnected European gas grid. Industry stakeholders argue these requirements are discriminatory and inconsistent with the accepted EU principle of mass balance.

Legal Analysis

The legality of physical delivery requirements raises questions about compatibility with: RED II/III Article 27 which explicitly recognises mass balance; Article 34 TFEU (free movement of goods), as preventing mass-balance biomethane from other Member States from qualifying for domestic compliance may constitute discrimination; and proportionality, as successful examples (Gate, Zeebrugge) exist where mass balance has been implemented without compromising environmental integrity, suggesting that blanket physical delivery requirements may fail the proportionality test.

The position of the Dutch Government on the physical delivery requirement has led to the issue in 2024 of a detailed opinion from the EU Commission, which argues that the Dutch refusal to recognize cross-border mass-balancing via the gas grid contradicts EU law.

The Dutch Government has committed to implement mass balancing for bio-LNG if the European Commission explicitly confirms that it is permitted and required under EU law. As of January 2026, there has been no such confirmation from the Commission and no definitive CJEU ruling on this question. However, the legal risk is substantial. Industry stakeholders have explicitly argued that such requirements are discriminatory and inconsistent with RED II/III.

2.6 Other Challenges

Permitting procedures remain lengthy (2-3 years and longer in some Member States) and complex. Grid connection cost allocation varies widely across Member States: France (producers pay 40%, 60% socialised up to €600,000), Italy (80% producer, 20% socialised), Germany (network operator pays 75%, plant 25%). Grid connection delays are also a challenge with reform of connection management procedures necessary in many Member States.

Rabobank (2024) identifies permitting delays, feedstock sourcing challenges, lack of market harmonisation, and financial constraints as key obstacles. The EBA Biomethane Investment Outlook notes that approximately €101 million in planned investments were cancelled, suspended, or scaled back, primarily due to procedural delays and shifting policy landscapes. Recent Commission scrutiny of ISCC underlines the need for stronger verification standards.

Recent reforms in Italy illustrate how grid connection rules can rapidly change project economics. The 2026 Budget Law introduced a new framework under which transmission and distribution system operators must connect both new biomethane plants and converted biogas plants. Seventy percent of connection investment costs are now borne by network operators, with producers paying the remaining 30%,

while network operators must also cover 100% of metering and compression costs. This shift from an earlier framework in which Italian producers typically bore 80% of connection costs significantly improves the financial viability of biomethane projects and directly addresses previous industry concerns about unpredictable grid connection costs and timelines.

Developing a pan-European market for the by-products of biomethane production - primarily digestate (bio-fertiliser) and biogenic CO2—faces significant regulatory, logistical, and technical hurdles. While the EU aims for a circular economy, the "secondary" nature of these products means they are often entangled in complex cross-border trade restrictions and fragmented standards. National

laws, such as the Nitrates Directive, often limit the spreading of digestate on land, with varying definitions across borders of what constitutes a "RENURE" (REcovered Nitrogen from manURE) fertiliser.

3. National Support Mechanisms: Key Examples

E-CUBE (2024) notes that "new models of biomethane support mechanisms have begun to replace feed-in tariff systems, primarily based on consumption incentives," including transport GHG/renewable fuel quotas, gas grid blending obligations, and tax exemptions.

By end-2023, 1,510 biomethane plants were operational in Europe. The EBA Investment Outlook reveals a remarkable 7% increase in greenfield investments, with 85% of total capital (€24.2 billion) allocated to fully new plants. Nearly €1.3 billion is allocated to infrastructure upgrades, including bio-LNG for transport.

Top countries with planned investments:

Spain: €4.8 billion (17.3 TWh/year) - emerging export and maritime hub

Denmark: €3.14 billion (10.3 TWh/year) - largest exporter, maritime demand driver

United Kingdom: €2.43 billion (6.8 TWh/year) - significant exporter to EU

France: €1.71 billion (3.7 TWh/year) - largest producer by capacity, export-restricted

Italy: €1.31 billion (3.2 TWh/year) - CfD mechanism, Exceptional growth (96 plants by 2023, up from one in 2018), supported by a CfD mechanism from 2023 and a national target of around 60 TWh by 2030. Italy is also restructuring part of its PNRR-based support architecture: a draft decree implementing the sixth revision of the PNRR is expected to shift from tariff-based incentives to dedicated capital grant programmes for biomethane

Sweden: €1.16 billion (2.5 TWh/year) - transport-focused

Poland: €1.09 billion (3.1 TWh/year) - emerging market

Finland: €1.02 billion (2.0 TWh/year) - growing commitment

Greece: €1.01 billion (2.4 TWh/year) - infrastructure expansion

Netherlands: €0.89 billion (3.6 TWh/year) - second-largest exporter

4. Policy Recommendations

To transition from today's fragmented, subsidy-driven landscape to a liquid, pan-EU biomethane market, the EU and Member States must:

Remove national export restrictions: France's prohibition on liquefying subsidised biomethane for export and ex-domain-only GO exports should be eliminated. Member States should recognise that subsidised biomethane, once injected into the grid, can be allocated via mass balance to LNG terminals anywhere in the EU for liquefaction and bunkering, provided appropriate PoS and UDB tracking are in place.

Eliminate physical delivery requirements: Member States must fully recognise mass balance for domestic compliance where RED II/III permits it, relying on UDB and enhanced auditing for traceability rather than physical delivery requirements that may violate EU internal market principles.

Harmonise certification systems: Establish full interoperability between ERGaR and AIB systems, harmonise GO cancellation rules, integrate both with the Union Database, and eliminate ex-domain cancellation requirements.

Complete UDB implementation: Including full operationalisation of upstream raw material tracking and connection to all national GO registries. Recognise that UDB alone will not remove national restrictions unless accompanied by policy alignment or legal enforcement.

Commission guidance and enforcement: The European Commission should issue interpretative guidance clarifying that mass balance must be recognised for domestic compliance, that physical delivery requirements constitute improper transposition unless strictly justified, and that national rules must not discriminate against biomethane from other Member States. Where Member States maintain discriminatory requirements, the Commission should consider infringement proceedings.

Additional measures: Harmonise FuelEU Maritime compliance; establish EU-wide blending standards; scale up demand-side policies; streamline permitting and grid connection (€101 million in planned investments were cancelled primarily due to procedural delays); design subsidies compatible with cross-border trade; clarify regulatory treatment of bio-methane production by-products and sustain political commitment.

5. Conclusion: Pathways to a Pan-EU Biomethane Market

The path forward: The regulatory architecture is largely in place; €28 billion in committed capital demonstrates investor readiness. The challenge now is consistent implementation, harmonisation of national approaches, removal of national export barriers and discriminatory physical delivery requirements, streamlined permitting, and technical delivery of integrated certification and tracking

systems. With almost 900 biomethane plants expected to enter operation in the next five years and projected capacity reaching 7.3 bcm per year by 2030, the sector is on a credible trajectory-but achieving the REPowerEU target of 35 bcm by 2030 will require coordinated action to remove structural barriers to cross-border trade.

The contrast between export-oriented countries (Denmark, Belgium) versus domestically locked markets (France, Netherlands physical delivery requirements) demonstrates that policy choices-not technical constraints or environmental necessity-determine whether biomethane contributes to a genuinely pan-European market. The legality of such restrictions under EU law is increasingly open to question

and may require resolution through Commission guidance, infringement proceedings, or CJEU preliminary rulings. Eliminating these restrictions is essential for achieving the EU's 35 bcm target and delivering efficient maritime decarbonisation under FuelEU Maritime.

The aviation industry is under increasing pressure to reduce carbon emissions as global air travel continues to grow. SAF has emerged as a practical near-term pathway to decarbonize aviation and meet long-term climate targets. OXT’s patented MA technology offers a scalable, cost-effective route to produce drop-in, low-carbon SAF from a wide range of abundant and renewable feedstocks. Backed by decades of research, engineering, and process development, OXT has advanced its technology into a flexible platform that integrates well with internationally proven alcohol-to jet synthesis technologies as well as existing aviation infrastructure. The OXT technology offers tremendous feedstock flexibility, enabling use of diverse biomass and renewable resources.

OXT has developed and advanced technology, processes and engineering solutions in conjunction with various companies around the world. OXT has a legacy of innovation spanning nearly three decades. OXT’s advanced gas-to-alcohol technology transforms carbon containing gases—such as methane from landfills and low-value industrial waste gases into high-performance, low carbon, liquid fuels—including aviation. These fuels are fully compatible with existing transportation and industrial infrastructure, offering practical, scalable solutions for decarbonization. By harnessing underutilized gas, waste streams, and bio-derived sources, OXT creates a direct bridge between today’s energy demands and tomorrow’s lower-carbon future.

title: Swiss energy tech startup Metafuels secures €1.92M to scale aviation fuel production
description:
April 1, 2026·2 min read Joy Laoun News Editor, Vestbee Swiss energy tech startup Metafuels secures €1.92M to scale aviation fuel production Zurich-based energy technology firm Metafuels, which develops sustainable aviation fuel through the Aerobrew process, has secured a €1.92 million grant from the Netherlands Enterprise Agency under the GroenvermogenNL programme.
Founded in 2021 by Saurabh Kapoor, Leigh Hackett, and Ulrich Koss, Metafuels develops sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
The company has also installed a demonstration plant at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland to validate the aerobrew process.
The approach aims to provide a scalable, cost-efficient route to synthetic aviation fuel while significantly reducing lifecycle carbon emissions compared to conventional jet fuel.
It will support progress toward the project’s final investment decision and the first commercial-scale production of synthetic sustainable aviation fuel in Europe.

Swiss energy tech startup Metafuels secures €1.92M to scale aviation fuel production

Zurich-based energy technology firm Metafuels, which develops sustainable aviation fuel through the Aerobrew process, has secured a €1.92 million grant from the Netherlands Enterprise Agency under the GroenvermogenNL programme.

Founded in 2021 by Saurabh Kapoor, Leigh Hackett, and Ulrich Koss, Metafuels develops sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). The company’s core technology, Aerobrew, converts renewable methanol into synthetic jet fuel (e-SAF) that is compatible with existing aircraft and airport infrastructure.

The aerobrew process uses renewable feedstocks, including green hydrogen produced via water electrolysis powered by renewable electricity, and carbon sourced either from direct air capture or from biogenic biomass such as wood or miscanthus. Methanol produced from these inputs is then converted into synthetic jet fuel. The technology is designed for high carbon conversion efficiency, selectivity, and overall SAF yield.

Metafuels is developing its first commercial-scale facility, the Turbe project in Rotterdam, which is progressing through front-end engineering and design, permitting, and commercial planning, with a target for production around 2030.

The company has also installed a demonstration plant at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland to validate the aerobrew process. The approach aims to provide a scalable, cost-efficient route to synthetic aviation fuel while significantly reducing lifecycle carbon emissions compared to conventional jet fuel.

Details of the deal

The €1.92 million Dutch grant will enable Metafuels to advance the Turbe project in Rotterdam by funding front-end engineering and design, permitting, and commercial development activities. It will support progress toward the project’s final investment decision and the first commercial-scale production of synthetic sustainable aviation fuel in Europe.

text:
San Donato Milanese (Milan), 1 April 2026 - Today the European Investment Bank (EIB) and Eni signed a 15-year loan for €500 million to convert selected units of Eni’s Sannazzaro de’ Burgondi refinery, located in the Italian province of Pavia, into a biorefinery. The agreement was signed by EIB Vice-President Gelsomina Vigliotti and Eni CEO Claudio Descalzi.

The project involves converting the refinery’s Hydrocracker (HDC2) unit using Ecofining™ technology, and building a pre-treatment plant for waste materials like used cooking oils and animal fats, as well as waste from the agri-food industry, which comprise the main feedstock used by Enilive (Eni’s company devoted to achieving more sustainable mobility) to produce hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) biofuels.

With its proprietary Ecofining™ technology, Enilive produces HVO – a biofuel made from renewable feedstocks (pursuant to the EU Renewable Energy Directive) such as used cooking oils and waste from the agri-food industry. Pure HVO can be used in approved engines, and is already available at more than 1 600 Enilive service stations across Europe. From 2028, the Sannazzaro plant will start producing HVO diesel biofuels and the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) biojet, with a production capacity of around 550 000 tonnes per year.

Building on existing utilities and infrastructure, the project will complement conventional fuel production with HVO diesel biofuels and SAF, helping reduce the carbon footprint of transport and decarbonise the aviation sector, for which SAF is currently the only available solution. By diversifying the product offering on the market, the project will also strengthen Italian and EU energy security, and serve the objectives of REPowerEU by expanding Europe’s biofuel production capacity.

The project follows a €500 million financing agreement signed in July 2025 to convert Eni’s Livorno refinery into a biorefinery. Transforming part of the Sannazzaro de’ Burgondi refinery as well pursues Enilive’s strategic objective: increasing biofuel production capacity to 5 million tonnes by 2030, including over 2 million tonnes of SAF production capacity. Biofuels are currently produced at Enilive’s biorefineries in Venice and Gela, and at the St Bernard Renewables LLC biorefinery in Louisiana in the United States (a joint venture in which Enilive holds a 50% stake). These will be joined in 2026 by Italy’s third biorefinery in Livorno, followed by two biorefineries currently under construction in Malaysia and South Korea. A fourth biorefinery in Italy, in Priolo, Sicily, will be developed together with Q8 by 2028.

“This financing represents strategic support for a project with high environmental and industrial value, contributing to the decarbonisation of the transport sector, particularly aviation. Through this initiative, the EIB aims to strengthen Europe’s capacity to produce advanced fuels and to promote the circular and sustainable use of resources,” said EIB Vice-President Gelsomina Vigliotti.

Eni CEO Claudio Descalzi said, “This new agreement with the EIB demonstrates the effectiveness and robustness of the strategy we pursue through our businesses related to the energy transition. To deliver a tangible transition towards energy solutions that have an increasingly low environmental impact, it is essential to create businesses that can grow and generate value. We achieve this by combining technology and the ability to deliver industrial-scale projects on the one hand, with a broad and growing customer base on the other. We see biorefining and biofuels as a fundamental component to support the progressive decarbonisation of transport – applicable across all segments of the sector, and already well aligned with existing demand. We are the second largest producer of biofuels in Europe and are working on three refinery conversions in Italy. This follows the completion of two others in Venice and Gela, which are already making a major contribution towards a more environmentally sustainable supply for the transport sector.”

Demand for SAF, driven by the blending mandates of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, is expected to grow rapidly from 2030 onwards – underpinning the technical and economic robustness of the initiative and its long-term sustainability. HVO biofuels play a key role, as they can deliver an immediate contribution to emissions reduction along value chains for the entire transport sector, including aviation, road, maritime and rail transport.

The conversion of the Sannazzaro site is consistent with the strategy of Eni and Enilive to increase biofuel production in response to growing demand in Europe and Italy, both to meet the emissions reduction targets set out in the Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), and to comply with Italian regulations on placing pure biofuels on the market. In 2024 biofuels accounted for 4% of worldwide energy consumption in transport, and are expected to reach 9% by 2035 and 12% by 2050, based on the IEA Net Zero scenario of the World Energy Outlook 2025.

Background information

Eni is a global energy tech company present in 62 countries, with over 32,000 employees, integrated along the entire value chain. Eni aims to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050 through the progressive decarbonisation of its processes and products. To reach this goal, the company has invested for over a decade in the research, development and application of game-changing technologies which can accelerate the transition towards increasingly sustainable solutions. These include carbon capture and storage (CCS) and fusion energy, a breakthrough that could enable the future generation of safe, virtually unlimited and zero-emission energy. Eni is a leader in supercomputing, a fundamental lever for competitiveness: Eni’s supercomputer ranks among the most powerful systems in the world, and the company is already committed to the new technological frontier of quantum computing. Eni’s traditional hydrocarbon exploration and production activities continue to generate value, supporting the transition while ensuring energy security through the diversification of sources.

EIB Group

The European Investment Bank Group is the financing arm of the European Union, owned by the 27 Member States, and one of the largest multilateral development banks in the world. In 2025, the EIB Group signed €100 billion of new financing and advisory services for over 870 high-impact projects under eight core priorities that support EU policy objectives: climate action and the environment, digitalisation and technological innovation, security and defence, territorial cohesion, agriculture and the bioeconomy, social infrastructure, strong global partnerships, and the savings and investments union. Beyond long-term loans for large infrastructure, the EIB Group crowds in private investment for high-risk innovative projects and businesses, with a growing role in Europe’s markets for venture debt, venture capital, guarantees and securitisations.

The European Investment Fund (EIF) is the subsidiary of the EIB Group specialised in providing guarantees and equity to improve access to finance for small and medium-sized businesses and startups across Europe. Acting as an anchor investor, through its extensive network of partnering banks and investment funds, the EIF mobilises private investment and nurtures the ecosystem of venture capital funds to support innovative European entrepreneurs.

title: Environmental groups urge German gov't to scrap plans to cut aviation tax
description:
Environmental groups have criticised the German government's plans to lower aviation tax, calling the move ecologically counterproductive and fiscally irresponsible, according to a joint letter to chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The federal cabinet today (1 April) approved a draft law that would reduce air passenger tax rates to the level they were before May 2024, reversing an increase introduced by the previous government.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced the plan last year, saying the move would boost the country’s aviation sector.
“Reducing the air passenger tax is ecologically counterproductive, economically ineffective, and fiscally irresponsible,” the groups said, adding that it burdens the federal budget and weakens an important climate policy instrument.
“The reduction of the air traffic tax is an important first step to ensure that 2026 becomes the comeback year for German aviation.”
text:
Environmental groups have criticised the German government's plans to lower aviation tax, calling the move ecologically counterproductive and fiscally irresponsible, according to a joint letter to chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The federal cabinet today (1 April) approved a draft law that would reduce air passenger tax rates to the level they were before May 2024, reversing an increase introduced by the previous government. The finance ministry said it was “important that these reductions are passed on to passengers”. Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced the plan last year, saying the move would boost the country’s aviation sector.

Germanwatch, sustainable mobility group VCD, and Bundesvereinigung gegen Fluglärm (BVF), a group focussing on reducing the harmful effects of air traffic, called on the government to halt the draft legislation, however, arguing against the tax cut from “a climate policy perspective and given the current economic and fiscal situation”.

“Reducing the air passenger tax is ecologically counterproductive, economically ineffective, and fiscally irresponsible,” the groups said, adding that it burdens the federal budget and weakens an important climate policy instrument. At the same time, it is questionable from a social and distributional policy perspective, and provides only sporadic and unsustainable relief to the aviation industry, they said.

The tax reduction, scheduled to go into effect on 1 July, would result in reduced revenue of some 200 million euros this year and around 350 million euros annually thereafter, they noted. Pointing out that some 70 percent of the population either does not fly at all or only once a year, the NGOs said reduced tax revenue would make it impossible to provide targeted relief to broad segments of the population in other areas. Electricity prices, already hiking as a result of the current international energy crisis, were one example of where such funds could be better directed, they said.

The groups described air traffic as “the most climate-damaging mode of transport and, at the same time, structurally privileged: kerosene is tax-free, and international flights are exempt from VAT and emissions trading.” The air passenger tax, alongside the intra-European emissions trading system, is “one of the few instruments that internalises at least some of the external environmental costs,” they said.

Boris Rhein, premier of the state of Hesse, home to Germany’s largest airport in Frankfurt, welcomed the move. “The reduction of the air traffic tax is an important first step to ensure that 2026 becomes the comeback year for German aviation.”

text:
The Namibia Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) and the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) officially launched a six-month feasibility study to assess the potential for a domestic Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) industry.

The launch event, held in Windhoek brought together international experts and local stakeholders to determine if Namibia can produce its own eco-friendly jet fuel.

The initiative is part of ICAO’s Assistance, Capacity-building and Training for Sustainable Aviation Fuels (ACT-SAF) Program, under the “No Country Left Behind” drive, and is supported by funding from Switzerland.

In a keynote address delivered on her behalf, NCAA Executive Director Toska Sem noted that over the next six months, the feasibility study will evaluate Namibia’s readiness across key areas, including policy and regulatory frameworks, sustainable feedstock availability, infrastructure capacity, and investment potential.

“Namibia’s selection for this program is the result of deliberate national effort in the country’s commitment to sustainable aviation,” she said.

The keynote highlighted that through initiatives such as the Namibia Green Hydrogen Program, Namibia is positioning itself as a future hub for clean energy production, noting that companies such as Cleanergy Solutions Namibia are already pioneering green hydrogen developments that could serve as a foundation for SAF production pathways.

“Climate responsibility is not an obligation, it is a choice rooted in our values, and in our vision for sustainable development,” she emphasized.

According to the NCAA, Namibia has maintained a ‘steadfast’ approach to sustainable flight, transitioning from its 2017 voluntary commitment to the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation to its 2024 integration into the ACT-SAF program.

The outcome of the study, meanwhile, will be clear: a practical, evidence-based roadmap tailored to Namibia’s unique context, Sem noted.

text:
Google has signed a long-term agreement with American Express Global Business Travel and Shell Aviation to continue sourcing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) through the Avelia platform, as part of efforts to reduce emissions from air travel, ESGtoday reported.

The deal extends Google’s participation in the Avelia program, which it joined in 2023. The platform, launched in 2022, allows companies to support the use of SAF through a system where they can pay for cleaner fuel and claim its environmental benefits, even if it is not physically used on their specific flights.

The Avelia system was developed by Shell and Accenture with support from the Energy Web Foundation. It also brings together demand from thousands of corporate clients through Amex GBT’s travel management services.

Google said SAF plays a key role in reducing emissions from the aviation sector, where cutting carbon output remains a challenge. The company added that long-term agreements like this can help increase demand and availability of cleaner fuels.

Since its launch, the Avelia platform has been adopted by 66 companies and airlines and has helped reduce more than 590,000 tonnes of carbon emissions.

The partners have also expanded the platform to allow multiple fuel suppliers, moving away from reliance on a single provider. They are exploring a system that would let airlines manage their own SAF supplies through the platform, improving tracking and transparency.

Shell Aviation said continued support from companies like Google is important for building the market for sustainable aviation fuel and encouraging wider adoption across the industry.

text:
The Swiss startup’s Turbe project at the Evos terminal in the Port of Rotterdam will be the first commercial deployment of its aerobrew methanol-to-jet technology, and a blueprint for large-scale e-SAF production across Europe.

Metafuels, the Swiss aviation technology company developing synthetic sustainable aviation fuel, has been awarded €1.92 million in grant funding from the Netherlands Enterprise Agency under its TSE Industry Studies, Hydrogen & Green Chemistry programme (GroenvermogenNL).

The grant goes to Metafuels’ Dutch subsidiary, Metafuels Nederland B.V., to advance the development of the Turbe project, the company’s first commercial e-SAF facility, located at the Evos terminal in the Port of Rotterdam.

The funding covers front-end engineering and design (FEED), permitting and consents, and commercial preparation ahead of a final investment decision (FID) targeted for mid-2026.

Metafuels’ core technology, aerobrew, converts renewable methanol into drop-in jet fuel using a methanol-to-jet process the company says delivers up to 90% lower lifecycle emissions than conventional kerosene, with no modifications required to existing aircraft or airport infrastructure.

FEED on the Turbe project was awarded to engineering and construction firm McDermott in December 2025. Turbe is designed to initially produce 12,000 litres of e-SAF per day, with a second phase planned to increase production tenfold to 120,000 litres per day.

Production is targeted from 2030, aligned with the point at which EU ReFuelEU Aviation synthetic fuel sub-mandates begin.

The Rotterdam location is not incidental. The Port of Rotterdam is Europe’s largest port and the Evos terminal is a dedicated multimodal methanol hub, the largest ethanol storage provider on the continent — giving

Metafuels access to the renewable methanol supply chain, logistics infrastructure, and industrial expertise it needs to make the project viable. The Turbe facility is intended as a blueprint for subsequent large-scale e-SAF plants.

The Netherlands Enterprise Agency grant supports the project development phase ahead of the investment decision; it does not fund construction.

Metafuels has now raised over $46 million in total, including a $24 million round led by UVC Partners announced in February 2026 (with Energy Impact Partners, Contrarian Ventures, RockCreek, Verve Ventures, and Fortescue Ventures), a $5 million grant from the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, and prior equity rounds.

The company is headquartered in Zurich and led by CEO Saurabh Kapoor. Metafuels also has a planned facility in Denmark (Pizol) and is preparing a demonstration plant at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland.

title: Latin America's sustainable potential meets reality - Air Cargo Week
description:

Latin America could supply 10 to 15 percent of global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) by 2050, potentially positioning the region as a leader in airfreight’s decarbonisation efforts.

text:
Latin America has strong SAF potential, with abundant feedstocks and supportive geography, but scaling production requires around US$204 billion in investment, coordinated regulation across countries and acceptance of higher fuel costs.

Early use cases, such as LATAM Cargo Colombia’s Valentine’s 2026 flower shipments, demonstrate up to 75 percent emissions reductions, yet deployment remains limited to high-margin, time-sensitive cargo rather than widespread adoption.

Policy frameworks and airport sustainability initiatives are advancing, but a significant gap persists between ambition and reality due to limited production capacity, funding constraints and the price premium of SAF over conventional jet fuel.

Latin America could supply 10 to 15 percent of global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) by 2050, potentially positioning the region as a leader in airfreight’s decarbonisation efforts. But at the moment that’s just a projection. We don’t have a crystal ball and the reality is a bit smaller. South America has the raw materials and the geography. The policy frameworks are taking shape, but turning potential into production means finding US$204 billion, aligning six countries on pricing and regulation, and absorbing higher fuel costs while the infrastructure catches up. That said, there is progress, just not yet at scale.

Resources without refineries

Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru and Chile all sit on the right raw materials for sustainable aviation fuel production. Sugarcane-based ethanol, palm oil and soybean-based hydro-processed esters work in current engines without need for modifications and cut lifecycle emissions by up to 75 percent. MIT researchers estimate that hitting 65 percent SAF use across the region by 2050 would reduce aviation emissions by about 60 percent. Getting there means building US$204 billion worth of production plants between now and then, with Brazil accounting for US$84 billion of that total. The resources are there. The capital isn’t, at least not yet.

From potential to practice

A few operations show what scaled

SAF use could look like. During Valentine’s 2026, LATAM Cargo Colombia, Kuehne+Nagel and The Elite Flower used over 130,800 litres of SAF to move

469.8 tonnes of Colombian flowers from Bogotá to Miami, cutting an estimated 300 tonnes of CO2e. The flowers arrived on schedule, cold-chain intact, emissions down 75 percent. It worked because the economics checked out for premium perishables during peak season. But that’s not the same as year-round deployment across general cargo.

Brazil introduced its Fuel of the Future Law in 2024, mandating one percent emissions reduction by 2027 and scaling to 10 percentby 2037.

Chile announced its Vuelo Limpio roadmap targeting 50 percent SAF contribution by 2050. Both are commitments, not aspirations. That said, both depend on production capacity that doesn’t exist yet.

Beyond fuel

But airports aren’t waiting for SAF plants to get built. Over 100 airports across 16 countries now hold Airport Carbon Accreditation, tracking and cutting emissions where they can control them directly. Quito International Airport became the first in the region to hit Level 4+, committing to zero operational emissions by 2035. Galápagos Ecological Airport was the world’s first built entirely under sustainability criteria, running on renewable energy with biodigesters that handle organic waste. Mexico covers the most ground with 45 airports in carbon programmes, backed by solar installations and electric ground vehicles.

Cost

Conventional jet fuel in Latin America costs about US$0.70 per litre. SAF costs between US$1.11 and US$2.86 per litre, depending on source and production method. And that gap doesn’t close without subsidies, carbon pricing or fuel blend mandates. Most Latin American governments haven’t committed to any of those at scale. Airlines and forwarders either absorb the premium or pass it to shippers. For now, SAF gets deployed where margins justify it, which means peak-season perishables and corporate sustainability programmes, but not baseline cargo operations.

Infrastructure meets ambition

South America’s path to decarbonisation isn’t speculation. The raw materials are there, the technology is proven and the policies are beginning to take shape. What’s missing is the capital, coordination and willingness to shoulder higher costs during this transition period. But airfreight can’t wait decades, and it can’t decarbonise without infrastructure that isn’t built yet. The gap is closing, just slower than commitments suggest.

text:
Deutsche Aircraft has advanced the development of its D328eco regional turboprop by deploying an integrated, model based digital engineering environment built on Dassault Systèmes’ 3DEXPERIENCE platform. The move marks a significant program milestone and strengthens the company’s strategy to industrialize the D328eco using a modern, data driven development and production ecosystem.

The D328eco, a next generation evolution of the Dornier 328, is being designed for short and medium range operations with upgraded performance, modern avionics, and full compatibility with sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). By incorporating virtual design, simulation, and validation early in the program, Deutsche Aircraft can assess system behavior, structural loads, and cabin configurations before physical manufacturing begins. This approach supports risk reduction, accelerates decision cycles, and helps maintain development timelines as the program progresses toward industrial maturity.

“Establishing a robust digital engineering platform is vital for the entire lifecycle of the D328eco to fulfill customer expectations," sats Nico Neumann, CEO of Deutsche Aircraft. "The 3DEXPERIENCE platform facilitates cross-functional collaboration and equips our teams with the solutions necessary to develop, manufacture, and maintain next-generation regional aircraft."

By centralizing product requirements, configuration management, and engineering data, Deutsche Aircraft ensures continuity between design, manufacturing, and service support. This digital backbone is particularly important as the company prepares for industrial ramp up at its new Final Assembly Line in Leipzig, where digitalized workflows will help enable a scalable and repeatable production system.

To further strengthen stakeholder engagement, Deutsche Aircraft is pushing for more digital innovation using Dassault Systèmes’ 3DLive application connected to Apple Vision Pro. The solution enables the user to experience a virtual D328eco model or a virtual twin within a mixed-realistic environments. Use cases include reviewing cabin layouts, evaluating design options and rehearsing operational procedures, all using real time program data derived from the actual aircraft’s digital mock-up (DMU).

“This technology enables clearer communication, faster alignment, and a shared understanding of the aircraft across all partners,” Neumann added. “It represents an important step in how modern aircraft are developed and supported and reinforces our commitment to bringing the D328eco to market as a next generation regional aircraft built in Germany.”

title: New Mexico Clean Transportation Fuel Program: New Market Opportunity for Biofuels
description:
On Jan. 22, the New Mexico Environmental Improvement Board unanimously approved a slightly revised version of the Clean Transportation Fuel Program regulations proposed by the New Mexico Environment Department.
New Mexico is the first state outside of the Pacific Coast Collaborative to adopt a clean fuels program, and the first major oil- and gas-producing state to adopt a program.
In other clean fuel programs, this type of power sourcing is generally restricted to electricity used to charge electric vehicles.
To my knowledge, the very first stakeholder to advance the concept of a clean fuel program for New Mexico was Virginia Smith of Adelante Consulting.
Based on that analysis, Adelante determined that a clean fuel program would be the most advantageous policy structure to create market demand for biomass.
text:
On Jan. 22, the New Mexico Environmental Improvement Board unanimously approved a slightly revised version of the Clean Transportation Fuel Program regulations proposed by the New Mexico Environment Department. The newly approved program mandates the fastest carbon intensity reduction in the U.S.: 20% by 2030, starting in April. New Mexico is the first state outside of the Pacific Coast Collaborative to adopt a clean fuels program, and the first major oil- and gas-producing state to adopt a program.

During the proceedings, New Mexico set a new gold standard for both stakeholder engagement and maximal integration of stakeholder recommendations. The state’s rulemaking process is extraordinary in that stakeholders are allowed to participate as active parties in the rulemaking. The New Mexico Environment Department was the petitioner with the burden to make the case to the board that the proposed regulations should be approved. Parties in this type of New Mexico rulemaking have the right to give opening and closing arguments, present witnesses, cross-examine the petitioner’s and other parties’ witnesses, present rebuttal testimony and file motions.

The rulemaking proceeded in distinct phases. It was initiated when the Environment Department filed a petition and the first version of the proposed regulations. Parties could then file notices of appearance, notices of intent to testify and submit written testimony. Hearing Officer Felicia Orth then adeptly presided over a two-week session of contentious but cordial case-in-chief direct testimony and cross-examinations that were primarily conducted in person in Santa Fe, but with some witnesses, parties and attorneys participating remotely. The first nine days of hearings began in September and ended in October. Following a break for rebuttal testimony and motions, Hearing Officer Orth convened a one-week session of rebuttal testimony and cross-examinations in November. Closing arguments and legal briefs were due in late December. In January, the board held three days of deliberations that examined every aspect of the program, and ultimately the board approved the final version of the proposed regulations with only minor revisions.

Parties in the rulemaking included New Mexico Oil & Gas Association, the Coalition for Clean Affordable Energy, Oxy USA, HF Sinclair, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, RNG Coalition, Food & Water Watch, Southwest Airlines, Low Carbon Fuels Coalition, Growth Energy, Rio Valley Biofuels and several individuals appearing pro se. Along with experienced New Mexico co-counsel Anne Minard, I had the privilege of representing Infinium Operations LLC, Verde Clean Fuels Inc. and the SAF Producer Group, which includes Gevo, NEXT Renewable Fuels Inc. and World Energy LLC.

Subsequent to the filing of the petition and at multiple junctures in the rulemaking, the Environment Department made revisions to the proposed regulations based on the testimony, evidence and arguments that had been presented. After a robust public process and many months of pre-hearing meetings with stakeholders and the hearings before the board, the Environment Department crafted a groundbreaking southwestern clean fuel program with many unique components.

On the final day of the rebuttal proceedings, NMED Climate Branch Chief Claudia Borchert was asked whether, after a week of rebuttal and cross-examination, she still had confidence in the final version of the regulations that she and the NMED rulemaking team had developed. Borchert said she was confident, citing her team as the primary reason: “I have a stellar team, and I think we really complement each other” (Tr. Vol. XIII, 4387:15-4388:1). She went on to state: “We’ve had, between the four years of trying to get it passed in the Legislature, and the 18-plus months of actually digging down and trying to understand it and all the conversations that have happened, it just means that the product, 113, NMED Exhibit 113, the rebuttal rule, has just gone through the ringer so many times that I do feel confident in it” (Tr. Vol. XIII, 4389:3-12).

The rule approved by the board includes multiple favorable provisions that expand the borders for clean fuel production, including:

• Book-and-claim provisions for renewable electricity and renewable natural gas that will enable clean fuel producers to achieve lower carbon intensity through the acquisition of low-CI process energy and heat

• A broad synthetic fuel definition and opportunities for synthetic fuels to opt in to the program

• Recognition of avoided methane emissions in pathway scores

• Favorable sustainable aviation fuel crediting based on a fixed carbon intensity (CI) benchmark score for alternative jet fuel that will enable 10 CI points more credit than diesel in 2030 and 20 CI points more in 2040, along with fueling supply equipment crediting for AJF

Unfortunately for the biomass power industry, the New Mexico CTFP regulations define “renewable electricity” to include only electricity generated by solar, wind, hydropower or geothermal generation. Under Section 206(E) of the regulations, qualifying renewable electricity sources have a zero carbon intensity score. Offsite renewable electricity sourcing can be done via the purchase of renewable energy certificates, typically referred to as RECs, that represent the carbon intensity of the power. In other clean fuel programs, this type of power sourcing is generally restricted to electricity used to charge electric vehicles. The New Mexico CTFP is the first clean fuel program to expand this power sourcing via RECs to liquid fuel production facilities that produce ethanol, biodiesel, renewable diesel or other qualifying low-carbon fuels.

As a strong supporter of clean fuel programs, it has been a privilege to participate in the establishment and development of the New Mexico CTFP. To my knowledge, the very first stakeholder to advance the concept of a clean fuel program for New Mexico was Virginia Smith of Adelante Consulting. Adelante had done analysis for a county in New Mexico to identify a policy that would create a market for the woody biomass generated by wildfire risk reduction treatments. Based on that analysis, Adelante determined that a clean fuel program would be the most advantageous policy structure to create market demand for biomass. Smith reached out to the Low Carbon Fuels Coalition in 2020 to request our help in getting a bill introduced. I am proud to report that the LCFC rose to that challenge and worked for five years to support its passage, with success finally being achieved by Executive Director Robin Vercruse and Chair Lindsay Fitzgerald in 2024.

The program’s adoption marks a significant expansion of clean fuel policy beyond coastal markets, and underscores the growing role of interior states in shaping the future of low-carbon fuel development

title: A hydrogen plant in Iceland will couple geothermal energy and solid-oxide electrolysis
description:
A new demonstration facility in northern Iceland will integrate geothermal energy with a solid-oxide electrolyzer cell (SOEC) to produce green hydrogen, representing a key step toward lower-cost sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
This Thermal Hybrid Production System, developed by Syntholene Energy Corp. (Chicago, Ill.; www.syntholene.com), takes advantage of the “significant thermal energy stored in geothermal fluid to produce ultra-pure steam at exactly the right temperature and pressure required for input to industrial SOEC modules,” explains Jack Williams, head engineer at Syntholene.
The geothermal fluid enters the system at high pressure as the hot-side input into Syntholene’s novel configuration of high-efficiency heat exchangers, transferring heat to ultra-pure water.
Since the same geothermal fluid generates the power required by the SOEC module, it provides both the required heat and electricity to produce hydrogen.
The technology has been demonstrated at the laboratory scale at Idaho National Laboratory (www.inl.gov), and is now being integrated with a live geothermal resource in Húsavík, Iceland, to demonstrate hydrogen production at industrially relevant scales, which Williams says will help to validate that “direct integration of geothermal energy with high-temperature SOEC technology can materially reduce the cost of hydrogen production.”
text:
A new demonstration facility in northern Iceland will integrate geothermal energy with a solid-oxide electrolyzer cell (SOEC) to produce green hydrogen, representing a key step toward lower-cost sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). This Thermal Hybrid Production System, developed by Syntholene Energy Corp. (Chicago, Ill.; www.syntholene.com), takes advantage of the “significant thermal energy stored in geothermal fluid to produce ultra-pure steam at exactly the right temperature and pressure required for input to industrial SOEC modules,” explains Jack Williams, head engineer at Syntholene.

The geothermal fluid enters the system at high pressure as the hot-side input into Syntholene’s novel configuration of high-efficiency heat exchangers, transferring heat to ultra-pure water. Since the same geothermal fluid generates the power required by the SOEC module, it provides both the required heat and electricity to produce hydrogen. External energy inputs for steam generation are a considerable cost in SOEC plants, and conventional SAF plants often couple their electrolyzer systems to intermittent power sources, such as wind and solar. “Individually, neither geothermal energy nor SOEC technology provides a decisive advantage, but their direct integration is transformative: geothermal fluid allows production of inherently low-cost steam with no additional heat input, enabling the SOEC’s roughly one-third lower electricity demand per kilogram of hydrogen to translate directly into reduced levelized cost of hydrogen,” says Williams.

The technology has been demonstrated at the laboratory scale at Idaho National Laboratory (www.inl.gov), and is now being integrated with a live geothermal resource in Húsavík, Iceland, to demonstrate hydrogen production at industrially relevant scales, which Williams says will help to validate that “direct integration of geothermal energy with high-temperature SOEC technology can materially reduce the cost of hydrogen production.”

text:
IATA urges EU ETS review – Calls for full CORSIA implementation, elimination of overlapping rules, and reinvestment of EU ETS revenues into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and decarbonisation technologies to protect European aviation competitiveness.

Support for SAF and investment certainty – Advocates a “book-and-claim” system for SAF to enable purchase-based claims, boost transparency, prevent double-counting, and create a level playing field across Europe.

Balance climate ambition with resilience – Warns that unchecked EU ETS costs could weaken connectivity, limit consumer choice, and divert investment from decarbonisation, emphasising harmonised policy aligned with global standards.

The International Air Transport Association (IATA) has called on the European Union to conduct a comprehensive review of its Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), highlighting the need to protect European air connectivity while supporting the sector’s decarbonisation goals.

IATA warns that without careful alignment, the EU ETS could undermine Europe’s aviation competitiveness, increase costs for airlines, and limit investment in sustainable solutions.

“European aviation policy must bolster competitiveness as it advances decarbonisation,” said Willie Walsh, IATA Director General. “Reviewing the EU ETS offers a critical opportunity to focus on cost-effective emission reductions. The priority must be the full implementation of CORSIA, the reinvestment of EU ETS revenues into sustainable aviation fuel and other credible decarbonisation solutions, and the removal of overlapping measures that add cost and complexity without environmental benefit. This is vital for preserving European air connectivity—a strategic asset for trade, integration, and commerce.”

Full CORSIA implementation

IATA stresses that the EU must fully implement the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) for all international flights, including routes within the European Economic Area. According to the association, layering regional measures on top of a global scheme adds administrative complexity and costs without providing additional climate benefits.

A harmonised framework, free from EU-specific eligibility rules for Eligible Emissions Units, is considered essential for predictable compliance and globally consistent environmental outcomes.

Book-and-claim

The trade body also urges the EU to enable a “book-and-claim” system for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), allowing airlines to claim environmental benefits based on purchases rather than the physical location of fuel use. IATA says this would enhance transparency, reduce double-counting, and create a level playing field for operators across Europe, while encouraging investment in SAF production.

The scheme would require amendments to the EU ETS Directive and the extension of the Union Database to track SAF movements and environmental attributes effectively.

Reinvesting ETS revenues

IATA highlights that aviation will surrender nearly 330 million EU ETS allowances between 2026 and 2030, generating billions for Member States. The association argues that a greater share of these funds should be reinvested into decarbonisation, particularly to scale SAF production and support emerging zero-emission technologies.

Current incentives, such as the SAF Allowance scheme, cover only a fraction of projected demand, meeting roughly 4–5% of the industry’s needs between 2026 and 2030. According to the EU’s Sustainable Transport Investment Plan, achieving SAF targets could require between €57 billion and €67 billion by 2035, rising to €268–€376 billion by 2050.
